content_voiceover: This slide maps normal body iron distribution and the duodenal absorption pathway. Total body iron is compartmentalized: about eighteen hundred milligrams in red blood cells, six hundred in reticuloendothelial macrophages, three hundred in bone marrow, and roughly a thousand in the liver as storage. All of this connects through a tiny circulating pool of transferrin-bound iron, only about three milligrams, turning over twenty to twenty-five milligrams a day, mostly from macrophage recycling of senescent RBCs. Net dietary absorption is just one to two milligrams a day, matching obligate iron loss, the basis of iron balance. On the right, dietary ferric iron is reduced by DCYTB to ferrous iron and taken up by DMT1 at the apical membrane, both upregulated by HIF-2 alpha under hypoxia. Inside the enterocyte, iron either stores as ferritin or exports basolaterally through ferroportin, oxidized by hephaestin or ceruloplasmin back to ferric iron for transferrin binding. Remember the absorption pearls: citric acid, vitamin C, and fructose enhance absorption, while tea polyphenols, bran phytate, calcium, and soy protein inhibit it, that's a classic point for patients on oral iron therapy.
keypoints: Transferrin pool tiny (~3mg) but turns over 20-25 mg/day via RBC recycling
Net absorption = obligate loss = 1-2 mg/day (iron balance)
Duodenum: DCYTB/DMT1 (apical uptake) → ferroportin (basolateral export), driven by HIF-2α
↑Absorption: vit C, citric acid, fructose; ↓absorption: tea, phytate, calcium, soy
keypoint_voiceover: Know the numbers: only one to two milligrams of iron is absorbed and lost daily, tiny compared to the twenty to twenty-five milligrams recycled internally from senescent red cells each day. At the duodenum, DCYTB and DMT1 bring iron in apically, ferroportin exports it basolaterally, and HIF-2 alpha upregulates both under hypoxia. For absorption, vitamin C and citric acid help, while tea, bran, calcium, and soy block it, a classic patient-counseling point.
